papers.full_text: Subjects Emerging infectious disease preparedness has traditionally focused on emergency medicine, infectious disease, and critical care specialists. However, the ophthalmologist is not insulated from emerging infectious disease. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak highlights why ophthalmologists should also be incorporated into outbreak surveillance and response. Throughout history, ophthalmologists have played an important role in identifying infectious diseases through their ocular manifestations. Yet, this role depends on a clear understanding of a pathogen’s ophthalmic phenotype. Despite growing attention surrounding the current Andes virus outbreak, the ocular manifestations of this pathogen remain largely undefined. This knowledge gap presents both an opportunity and a responsibility for ophthalmologists to systematically characterise ocular involvement and contribute to emerging infectious disease surveillance. Herein, we review the available evidence regarding ocular involvement in hantavirus infection and contend that ophthalmologists have a critical role in defining the ocular phenotype of Andes virus during the current outbreak. The Andes strain of Hantavirus was recently documented aboard an international vessel. In April 2026, passengers and crew aboard the MV Hondius, began developing severe respiratory illness during an itinerary across the South Atlantic. The World Health Organization was notified on May 2, 2026, and Andes virus was confirmed as the causative pathogen on May 5 [1]. As of late-May 2026, 13 confirmed or probable cases and 3 deaths had been reported across multiple countries, with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) monitoring several individuals across multiple US states [2]. Although the overall public health risk in the United States remains low, the CDC has issued a Health Alert Network advisory emphasising heightened clinical vigilance. Hantaviruses (family Hantaviridae) are enveloped, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA viruses transmitted primarily through aerosolisation of infected rodent excrement, causing two principal syndromes: hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) from New World hantaviruses including Sin Nombre and Andes viruses, and haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) from Old World hantaviruses such as Puumala, Hantaan, and Seoul viruses. Andes virus is the only hantavirus with recently confirmed person-to-person transmission, typically via respiratory secretions during prolonged close contact with a symptomatic individual [3]. The ophthalmic literature on hantavirus is dominated by Puumala virus, which causes nephropathia epidemica (NE), a generally mild to moderate, renal-predominant form of HFRS. In the largest prospective ophthalmic series to date, Hautala et al. examined 92 eyes of 46 serologically confirmed NE patients and found that 70% reported ocular symptoms during acute illness, with decreased IOP in 88%, reduced visual acuity in 87%, conjunctival chemosis in 87%, crystalline lens thickening in 82%, a myopic shift in 78%, anterior chamber shallowing in 64%, and shortened vitreous length in 52% [4]. All anterior segment changes resolved fully with systemic recovery. Transient myopia is the hallmark finding, occasionally exceeding −4.0 diopters [5]. External findings include periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, and subconjunctival haemorrhage [4,5,6]. Posterior findings are less frequent but include retinal haemorrhages, macular oedema, retinal whitening near the optic disc, and a self-limiting posterior necrotising retinitis, with neuro-ophthalmic manifestations possible when CNS complications such as hypophyseal haemorrhage occur [5]. Although ocular manifestations of Puumala strain of hantavirus infection are well described, virtually no ophthalmic data exist for Andes virus, the pathogen responsible for the current outbreak. This distinction is critical because existing ophthalmic knowledge is derived from a different virus, a different clinical syndrome, and a substantially different severity spectrum. What we do know is that in contrast to the Puumala virus, the systemic manifestations of the Andes virus causes HPS, a fulminant cardiopulmonary illness in which patients progress rapidly to respiratory failure, mechanical ventilation, and in severe cases extracorporeal support [7]. To date, no ophthalmic evaluation of HPS patients has been published. This gap in knowledge has practical consequences. Clinically, this means that the pattern of presentation that ophthalmologists may be tasked to recognise is extrapolated from a population that differs in virus, syndrome severity, and clinical state. The existing literature on the Puumala virus may be used to prompt suspicion (i.e., a febrile patient with bilateral unexplained myopic shift should raise the possibility of hantavirus), but it cannot yet tell ophthalmologists what Andes virus ocular disease looks like beyond that. The current outbreak represents not only a clinical challenge but also a scientific opportunity. For ophthalmologists, this means that every HPS patient managed at a US referral centre during the current outbreak who is well enough to undergo ophthalmic evaluation represents an opportunity to generate evidence that does not yet exist. A standardised assessment, documented and reported in the literature, would begin to answer a question that the existing literature cannot. Importantly, ophthalmologists should examine patients with known or suspected hantavirus using correct transmission-based precautions. Unlike other hantaviruses, Andes virus has documented person-to-person transmission via respiratory secretions, a characteristic with no known analogue among other hantaviruses. For ophthalmologists, this distinction is particularly relevant because slit-lamp examination requires prolonged face-to-face proximity. Consequently, infection-control preparedness should be considered. The CDC recommends airborne infection isolation with gown, gloves, eye protection, and an N95 or higher-level respirator for any patient with confirmed or suspected infection [2]. Historically, ophthalmologists have contributed immensely to the recognition and characterisation of systemic infectious diseases through their ocular manifestations. From syphilis and tuberculosis to more recent outbreaks involving Zika virus, Mpox, and COVID-19, ocular findings have occasionally provided diagnostic clues, insight into disease pathogenesis, and opportunities for longitudinal monitoring. The Andes virus should be viewed within this broader framework. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak carries with it a powerful lesson. We as ophthalmologists are not peripheral observers during emerging infectious disease events. We contribute to surveillance, diagnosis, characterisation of novel ocular manifestations, and implementation of appropriate infection-control practices. As the outbreak evolves, systematic ophthalmic evaluation of affected patients may help close a major knowledge gap regarding the ocular manifestations of the Hantavirus Andes strain infection. analysis.background: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak highlights that ophthalmologists are not insulated from emerging infectious diseases and that ocular manifestations of this pathogen remain largely undefined, creating a surveillance gap.
analysis.methods: The authors conducted a narrative review of existing literature on hantavirus ocular involvement, emphasizing the need for systematic ophthalmic assessment during the current outbreak.
analysis.results: No ophthalmic data exist for Andes virus (F23), whereas a large Puumala virus series reported ocular symptoms in 70% of patients, with decreased intra‑ocular pressure in 88% and transient myopia up to –4.0 D (F18, F20).
analysis.contribution: The paper argues that ophthalmologists can fill a critical knowledge gap by characterising the ocular phenotype of Andes virus, thereby enhancing outbreak surveillance and informing clinical vigilance.
analysis.limitations: The review notes the absence of any published ophthalmic evaluation of HPS patients caused by Andes virus, limiting conclusions to extrapolation from other hantavirus strains.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The 2026 Andes virus outbreak shows ophthalmologists are vulnerable and ocular signs are poorly defined. Methods: The authors reviewed existing hantavirus ophthalmic literature. Results: No ocular data exist for Andes virus, while a Puumala series found 70% ocular symptoms and up to –4.0 D transient myopia. Contribution: Ophthalmologists can generate needed evidence and improve surveillance. Limitations: No published ophthalmic evaluations of Andes‑virus HPS patients are available.

papers.title: Increasing spatial scale of analysis weakens and can mask the dilution effect for hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: Despite its major implications for biodiversity conservation and public health, the generality of a protective effect of biodiversity on zoonotic pathogen transmission (i.e., the dilution effect) remains strongly debated. This controversy may partly arise from the diversity of analytical approaches used, but also from the spatial scales at which studies are conducted. Here, we explicitly test whether increasing the spatial scale of analysis affects the detection of the relationship between hantavirus infection prevalence and rodent species richness, using a global dataset spanning multiple regions. Although the association between species richness and infection prevalence remains negative across all spatial scales, we show that the magnitude of the dilution effect progressively weakens as spatial aggregation increases and can become statistically non-significant at coarse spatial resolutions. These results, which are consistent across world regions, indicate that the dilution effect is likely a general feature of hantavirus-rodent systems, but that its empirical detection is highly sensitive to the spatial scale of analysis. Our findings highlight how large-scale spatial aggregation can mask underlying ecological processes and emphasize the need to carefully match spatial scale to the biological mechanisms under investigation when testing biodiversity-disease relationships. Finally, we discuss the ecological and methodological mechanisms that may obscure dilution effects and outline why scale-explicit approaches are essential for robust inference in biodiversity-disease research.

PLOS Global Public Health | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0007045 September 8, 2026 2 / 11 Introduction In the mid-twentieth century, the widespread use of vaccines and antibiotics substan­ tially reduced the burden of many infectious diseases and contributed to optimism about their future control [1]. However, this optimism has since been tempered by the steadily increasing frequency of emerging infections, illustrated by the examples of zoonotic diseases like Ebola virus in West Africa, Zika virus in South America, or, more recently the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) [2,3]. Moreover, these new threats seem to be closely linked to environmental issues such as climate change, land-use change and forest loss, because most of these emerging pathogens originate from wildlife [2]. To this extent, the potential link between the increased transmission of zoonotic pathogens and the reduction of vertebrate biodiversity clearly calls for investigating the possibility of using biodiversity conservation strategies as a public health oppor­ tunity [4–7]. Currently, much research focuses on the dilution effect theory, which suggests that a greater species richness within vertebrate communities (hereafter called hosts) can reduce (dilute) pathogen transmission [8,9] through several mech­ anisms [10]. First, the addition of non-competent host species, i.e., weakly or not at all involved in pathogen transmission within the ecosystem can theoretically reduce transmission of some pathogen species by decreasing contacts among competent host species [11]. However, a dilution effect can also be detected if the abundance of a species that strongly contributes to pathogen transmission, i.e., a highly com­ petent host, negatively correlates with host species richness [12]. It is nevertheless important to point out that a greater species richness within host communities could also increase pathogen prevalence, i.e., creating an amplification effect, and may be associated with enhanced risk of pathogen emergence [9]. Such amplification could also be associated with increases in pathogen richness in parallel with host species diversity [13]. The generality of dilution and amplification effects therefore remains strongly debated [9]. Empirical evidence suggests that the direction and strength of biodiversity-disease relationships can depend on multiple factors, including the composition and complexity of the vertebrate host communities [14–17]. Dilution and amplification processes may even occur concurrently within the same host-pathogen system [18]. As a result, it remains unclear under which ecological contexts dilution or amplification effects should be expected, and which mechanisms primarily drive these contrasting outcomes. Part of this ongoing debate may stem from methodological heterogeneity among studies, particularly differences in spatial scale, ecosystem type, and metrics used to quantify pathogen transmission [19–23]. Spatial scale is especially critical as ecological processes influencing host community structure and pathogen transmission occur at different spatial scales. Consequently, analyses conducted at mismatched or overly coarse spatial resolutions may obscure underlying biodiversity-disease relationships, contributing to apparently contrasting empirical results. Recent meta- analyses have highlighted the need to disentangle the relative influence of these factors when assessing the generality of dilution or amplification effects [15,17–19,24]. derived from the global hantavirus dataset described by Milholland et al. PLOS Global Public Health | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0007045 September 8, 2026 3 / 11 In this study, we test whether the relationship between host species richness and pathogen prevalence—negative under a dilution effect or positive under an amplification effect—depends on the spatial scale at which it is assessed. Beyond the direction of this relationship, our central focus is on its magnitude, i.e., on how strongly an additional rodent species reduces hantavirus prevalence, and on whether that magnitude is preserved as the unit of analysis is coarsened. Using a global scale-explicit re-analysis of a compiled dataset of hantavirus prevalence across rodent host communities, we quantify how systematic changes in the spatial extent of study areas modify the inferred relationship between biodi­ versity and pathogen prevalence. We specifically examine whether increasing spatial aggregation alters both the strength and the statistical detectability of biodiversity–disease relationships. Finally, we discuss the ecological and methodolog­ ical mechanisms that may obscure biodiversity–disease relationships and emphasize the need to adopt scale-explicit approaches, and to extend this scale-explicit framework to other host–pathogen systems. Materials and methods Biological model Orthohantaviruses (enveloped, single-stranded, negative sense, RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae) constitute a particularly suitable biological model to characterise the effect of spatial scale on dilution/amplification effect. Hantaviruses are transmitted by various rodent species of the superfamily Muroidea in Europe, Asia, and the Americas [25], which are habitat generalists, geographically widespread, and locally highly abundant, making them well suited for large-scale comparative analyses. Moreover, despite several hantaviruses that tend to use several hosts [26], hantavi­ ruses tend nevertheless to be “specialist”, i.e., associated with only one given small-mammal species (especially rodents, shrews, moles, and bats) For example, Puumala virus (PUUV) in Europe is essentially restricted to the bank vole Myodes glareolus, Sin Nombre virus (SNV) in North America is primarily carried by the deer mouse Peromyscus maniculatus, and Andes virus in southern South America is associated with the long-tailed pygmy rice rat Oligoryzomys longicaudatus. By contrast, Seoul virus (SEOV), the dominant hantavirus genotype in our Asian dataset, infects several commensal Rattus species, and Tula virus (TULV) in Europe circulates across multiple Microtus voles, so that some hantaviruses fit a “multi- host” pattern. The richness term we model here is total rodent species richness in the cell, rather than the richness of competent reservoirs only, because for most non-reservoir species hantavirus competence has not been quantitatively assessed in the literature compiled by Milholland et al. [26,27]; we revisit this point in the Discussion [28]. This host adap­ tation pattern yields a large variability in host competence within rodent communities. In this context, the dilution effect has been observed several times for these hantaviruses, being especially evident when host species richness is high with an associated decrease in relative abundance of the most susceptible host species [29,30]. Moreover, hantaviruses represent a significant threat to human health. Transmission to humans occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolized virus particles from infected rodent excreta or through direct contact with infected hosts, and can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (mainly in Asia and Europe) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (mainly in the Americas) [31]. Thus, identifying the ecological determinants of the relationship between hantavirus prevalence and host species richness is crucial for understanding and preventing zoonotic disease risk in human populations. Dataset The dataset used in this study is described by Milholland et al. [26,27]. In brief, this dataset comes from an extensive survey of the literature between 1971–2015 and comprises a global compilation of wild rodent species and their docu­ mented associations with hantaviruses. For each study, the dataset includes the number of individuals testing positive or negative for specific hantavirus species based on direct detection of viral genetic material (RNA). Accordingly, only host-virus associations confirmed by RT-PCR were retained. Although this molecular approach likely underestimates total host exposure compared to serology-based studies, it ensures a high specificity of host-virus associations by excluding PLOS Global Public Health | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0007045 September 8, 2026 4 / 11 serologic records in which specific hantavirus genotypes cannot be reliably identified. Therefore, data for each locality of the field study extracted involves sampling date, rodent species sampled, number of each hantavirus genotype iden­ tified within each rodent species, and total sample size for each rodent species. In total, the dataset contains exploitable data for three regions (North America, Asia, and Europe), encompassing 154 rodent species, 17,893 rodent individuals screened by RT-PCR (1,575 positives), and 19 hantavirus genotypes. A region-by-region breakdown of sampling effort, host species (including region-endemic species that tested positive), dominant hantavirus genotypes and main reservoir hosts is provided in S1 and S2 Tables. Statistical aggregation Spatial aggregation was performed using an equal-area hexagonal grid to ensure comparability of spatial units across lat­ itudes. This avoids geometric distortions inherent to latitude–longitude grids defined in degrees, in which cell area varies with latitude, and provides a consistent definition of spatial scale. Hexagons were generated separately for each region in a Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area (LAEA) projection centered on the mean longitude and latitude of that region’s sampling sites, in order to preserve cell area while minimising local distortion. Twelve grain sizes were evaluated, defined by the hexagon “diameter” (the distance between opposite vertices): 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600 and 800 km. These grains span roughly two orders of magnitude in area, from sub-landscape (≈10 km) to sub-continental (≈800 km), and were chosen because they bracket the spatial extents at which biotic interactions among rodent hosts and large- scale climatic constraints respectively dominate community assembly. For each region and each grain, only cells contain­ ing at least two rodent species and a non-zero sampling effort (N > 0) were retained in the analysis. Fig 1 displays the raw, unaggregated sampling sites (i.e., point coordinates from the source dataset, with no spatial pooling); aggregation into hexagonal cells was applied only to the statistical analysis underlying Fig 2. Spatial grain was systematically increased by varying hexagonal cell size, thereby pooling progressively larger areas while maintaining constant cell area within each resolution. This approach allows spatial scale to be interpreted unambigu­ ously in terms of area rather than angular distance. Fig 1. Spatial distribution of the sampling sites for Asia, Europe, and North America. Points are individual sampling localities from the source data­ set [26,27]; no spatial aggregation is applied here. The size of the circles increases with the rodent species richness measured and the color represents the prevalence observed. BR and AA are co-last authors on this work. * ana.vigueras09@gmail.com Abstract Despite its major implications for biodiversity conservation and public health, the gen­ erality of a protective effect of biodiversity on zoonotic pathogen transmission (i.e., the dilution effect) remains strongly debated. This controversy may partly arise from the diversity of analytical approaches used, but also from the spatial scales at which studies are conducted. Here, we explicitly test whether increasing the spatial scale of analysis affects the detection of the relationship between hantavirus infection preva­ lence and rodent species richness, using a global dataset spanning multiple regions. Although the association between species richness and infection prevalence remains negative across all spatial scales, we show that the magnitude of the dilution effect progressively weakens as spatial aggregation increases and can become statistically non-significant at coarse spatial resolutions. These results, which are consistent across world regions, indicate that the dilution effect is likely a general feature of hantavirus–rodent systems, but that its empirical detection is highly sensitive to the spatial scale of analysis. Our findings highlight how large-scale spatial aggregation can mask underlying ecological processes and emphasize the need to carefully match spatial scale to the biological mechanisms under investigation when testing biodiversity–disease relationships. Finally, we discuss the ecological and method­ ological mechanisms that may obscure dilution effects and outline why scale-explicit approaches are essential for robust inference in biodiversity-disease research. PLOS Global Public Health | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgph.0007045 September 8, 2026 2 / 11 Introduction In the mid-twentieth century, the widespread use of vaccines and antibiotics substan­ tially reduced the burden of many infectious diseases and contributed to optimism about their future control [1]. However, this optimism has since been tempered by the steadily increasing frequency of emerging infections, illustrated by the examples of zoonotic diseases like Ebola virus in West Africa, Zika virus in South America, or, more recently the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) [2,3]. Moreover, these new threats seem to be closely linked to environmental issues such as climate change, land-use change and forest loss, because most of these emerging pathogens originate from wildlife [2]. To this extent, the potential link between the increased transmission of zoonotic pathogens and the reduction of vertebrate biodiversity clearly calls for investigating the possibility of using biodiversity conservation strategies as a public health oppor­ tunity [4–7]. Currently, much research focuses on the dilution effect theory, which suggests that a greater species richness within vertebrate communities (hereafter called hosts) can reduce (dilute) pathogen transmission [8,9] through several mech­ anisms [10]. First, the addition of non-competent host species, i.e., weakly or not at all involved in pathogen transmission within the ecosystem can theoretically reduce transmission of some pathogen species by decreasing contacts among competent host species [11]. However, a dilution effect can also be detected if the abundance of a species that strongly contributes to pathogen transmission, i.e., a highly com­ petent host, negatively correlates with host species richness [12]. It is nevertheless important to point out that a greater species richness within host communities could also increase pathogen prevalence, i.e., creating an amplification effect, and may be associated with enhanced risk of pathogen emergence [9]. Such amplification could also be associated with increases in pathogen richness in parallel with host species diversity [13]. The generality of dilution and amplification effects therefore remains strongly debated [9]. Empirical evidence suggests that the direction and strength of biodiversity-disease relationships can depend on multiple factors, including the composition and complexity of the vertebrate host communities [14–17]. Dilution and amplification processes may even occur concurrently within the same host-pathogen system [18]. As a result, it remains unclear under which ecological contexts dilution or amplification effects should be expected, and which mechanisms primarily drive these contrasting outcomes. Part of this ongoing debate may stem from methodological heterogeneity among studies, particularly differences in spatial scale, ecosystem type, and metrics used to quantify pathogen transmission [19–23]. Spatial scale is especially critical as ecological processes influencing host community structure and pathogen transmission occur at different spatial scales. Consequently, analyses conducted at mismatched or overly coarse spatial resolutions may obscure underlying biodiversity-disease relationships, contributing to apparently contrasting empirical results. Recent meta- analyses have highlighted the need to disentangle the relative influence of these factors when assessing the generality of dilution or amplification effects [15,17–19,24]. derived from the global hantavirus dataset described by Milholland et al. papers.title: Emerging Global Health Challenges: Which Poses a Greater Threat, Ebola Virus or Hantavirus?
papers.abstract: The world is experiencing more epidemics today than at any point in recent history, yet global readiness to respond is steadily slipping backwards. Pandemic risks, unstable geopolitics, and rapidly changing ecosystems have begun to outpace the world’s ability to prepare, creating conditions where future outbreaks may become far harder to manage (Global Preparedness Monitoring Board, 2026). As the global health system weakens, emerging viruses such as Ebola and hantavirus are appearing more frequently and with greater severity; from Ebola surging in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda to hantavirus emerging unexpectedly on international cruise ships. In this rising landscape of vulnerability, which of these threats poses the greater global risk? To determine which virus poses the greater global risk, it is essential to examine how each behaves within a world that is increasingly unprepared for new outbreaks. Ebola typically enters human populations through contact with infected animals and then spreads efficiently through human-to-human transmission. Hantavirus, by contrast, is primarily transmitted from infected rodents to humans, with human-to-human spread occurring far less frequently (WHO, 2026) (WHO, 2025). Although both viruses are severe and potentially fatal, Ebola’s high transmissibility and mortality give it a clearer global threat profile, while hantavirus presents a different challenge: its symptoms often resemble mild illnesses, leading to delayed diagnosis and unpredictable detection patterns (BBC World Service, 2012). While Ebola and hantavirus differ in their transmission dynamics, both are classic examples of zoonotic diseases that underscore the importance of the One Health approach. Human encroachment into wildlife habitats, deforestation, agricultural expansion, biodiversity loss, and climate change continue to increase interactions between humans, wildlife, and animal reservoirs. These environmental changes facilitate the emergence and re-emergence of infectious diseases, making future spillover events increasingly likely. Consequently, strengthening collaboration among public health, veterinary, environmental, and wildlife sectors should become a central component of global preparedness strategies rather than a reactive response once outbreaks occur. Another important lesson from both Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks is that preparedness cannot be measured solely by the availability of vaccines or clinical treatment. Robust surveillance systems, rapid laboratory diagnosis, effective risk communication, trained public health personnel, and cross-border information sharing are equally critical. Many countries continue to struggle with fragmented surveillance systems and inadequate laboratory capacity, resulting in delayed outbreak detection and response. Investing in preparedness before outbreaks occur remains substantially more cost-effective than responding after epidemics have already spread. Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD), a severe form of Ebola, is currently affecting communities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. The virus is believed to originate from non-human primates or bats, and its rapid evolution raises growing concern. With no approved vaccines or specific treatments available, control efforts rely entirely on early case detection, isolation, and supportive care (WHO, 2026). Comparatively, the recent cruise ship–linked hantavirus outbreak was alarming because it travelled through 32 countries within a week, demonstrating how quickly even a rodent-borne virus can cross borders. However, WHO’s assessment indicates that the overall global risk remains relatively low: the Andes virus; the only hantavirus strain capable of human-to-human transmission, requires close and prolonged contact for spread. The danger of Hanta virus lies in delayed diagnoses (WHO, 2026). The question is not simply which virus poses more risk, but whether the world is prepared for what comes next? Both outbreaks could have been contained more effectively with stronger surveillance and preparedness systems, yet global capacity continues to erode, making timely public health responses increasingly difficult. Budget constraints have already forced major cutbacks, including a reduction in the WHO’s operating budget following the U.S. withdrawal, limiting the organisation’s ability to support outbreak response, early detection, and rapid containment (France 24, 2025). This decline in global readiness leaves the world increasingly vulnerable, regardless of whether the next threat emerges from Ebola, hantavirus, or an entirely new pathogen. Strengthening surveillance systems, investing in One Health approaches, and restoring sustainable global health financing should therefore become urgent international priorities before the next epidemic emerges.

papers.title: Generation and Characterization of the Human Anti-HTNV Antibody KJJ4
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) is the predominant causative agent of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in China, yet no specific antiviral therapy is currently available. Neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) represent a promising strategy, but most existing anti-HTNV NAbs are heterologous and carry immunogenicity risks. Here, two fully human antibodies from a previously established human anti-HTNV phage display library were generated and characterized. KJJ3, a VL-VL tandem antibody derived from clone 3–12, showed weak binding to inactivated HTNV and minimal neutralizing activity (IC50 = 27.12 μg/mL). However, KJJ4, an engineered IgG4 antibody derived from clone 4–19 and carrying the S108P hinge mutation to prevent Fab-arm exchange, bound inactivated HTNV antigen and recombinant glycoprotein Gn (residues 19–371) in a dose-dependent manner, with only weak binding to Gc. Surface plasmon resonance yielded an association rate constant of 4.70 × 103 M−1s−1, a dissociation rate constant of 3.06 × 10−3 s−1, and an equilibrium dissociation constant of 650 nM for monomeric Gn19–371. In a Vero E6 focus-reduction microneutralization assay, KJJ4 neutralized HTNV in vitro with an IC50 of 2.879 μg/mL. These data establish KJJ4 as a fully human anti-HTNV antibody with experimentally defined in vitro binding and neutralizing activity, warranting further evaluation in animal models of HTNV infection.

papers.title: Network-Guided Drug Repurposing for Hantavirus Infection: Pathway Analysis, Target Identification, and Molecular What-If Simulations
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses cause haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, together responsible for more than 200,000 cases annually, but no specific antiviral therapy is approved. We developed a three-stage computational framework for systematic drug repurposing. Transcriptomic analysis of Hantaan virus-infected human umbilical vein endothelial cells (GEO GSE133751) identified 203 differentially expressed genes dominated by interferon-stimulated genes. A STRING protein–protein interaction network (176 nodes, 3,210 edges) and composite master-regulator centrality score identified 15 hubs, including ISG15, IRF1, CXCL10, STAT1, and DDX58. Open Targets analysis identified six druggable hubs and 12 repurposing candidates in four priority tiers. An ordinary differential equation model of type I interferon signalling then evaluated eight drug perturbations. Early IFN-β achieved the fastest viral clearance (3.5 days) with reduced CXCL10 immunopathology. Early JAK inhibition delayed clearance (4.9 days) and increased CXCL10, an effect that follows from modelling CXCL10 as an IRF1-driven rather than STAT1-driven output. Combining IFN-β with an anti-CXCL10 monoclonal antibody produced the best balance between antiviral efficacy and immunopathology control, although in the present model the antiviral gain of this combination derives entirely from its interferon component. This mechanistically grounded, evidence-ranked framework prioritises candidate therapies and phase-specific combinations for preclinical hantavirus studies.

papers.title_zh: 基于网络的药物再利用用于 汉坦病毒 感染:通路分析、靶点识别与分子情景模拟

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒导致肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征,每年造成>200,000例病例,但尚无获批的抗病毒治疗方案。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者开发了一个三阶段的计算框架用于药物再利用,包括对汉滩病毒感染的人类脐静脉内皮细胞进行转录组分析(203个差异表达的干扰素刺激基因),构建STRING蛋白-蛋白相互作用网络(176个节点,3,210条边)以识别15个枢纽调控因子,Open Targets分析寻找六个可药物化的枢纽和12个再利用候选药物,以及一个I型干扰素信号通路的常微分方程模型来评估八种药物扰动。
analysis_zh.results: 早期IFN-β治疗最快清除病毒(3.5天),并降低了CXCL10相关免疫病理;相反,早期JAK抑制延迟了清除(4.9天)并增加了CXCL10;将IFN-β与抗CXCL10单抗联合使用实现了最佳的抗病毒-免疫病理平衡,尽管抗病毒效益仅来自干扰素成分。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该基于机制、按证据等级排序的框架优先考虑候选疗法和针对不同阶段的组合,用于预临床汉坦病毒研究。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告。

papers.title: Andes Hantavirus human-to-human transmission dynamics and1 preparedness scenarios
papers.abstract: Abstract Human-to-human transmission of the Andes virus (ANDV), which causes the deadly Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome, has been documented in several outbreaks, but remains insufficiently characterized to ensure preparedness against future emergence. Here, we integrate epidemiological data from historical outbreaks and from the 2026 MV Hondius outbreak with a stochastic network-based transmission model to quantify ANDV epidemic potential and control requirements. We estimate a reproduction number of R 0 = 2.30 (95% CI: 1.33–3.27), supporting sustained human transmission. Uncertainty and sensitivity analysis show that variation in transmissibility and incubation period mainly affects outbreak timing and size, while superspreading events can substantially alter the epidemic evolution. Model analysis and simulations further reveal how contact-network structure strongly modulates outbreak size, with close-contact clustering facilitating containment. Due to the virus characteristics, rapid identification and isolation can effectively suppress outbreaks, even more effectively than in the case of COVID-19, whereas pre-symptomatic transmission or increased mixing could substantially increase risk. Our results provide a quantitative framework for ANDV preparedness and highlight the most critical transmission features for future surveillance.

papers.title: Incidence, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, and pharmacological management of the 2026 Andes virus outbreak.
papers.abstract: Hantavirus is considered as a fatal zoonotic pathogen that can be commonly transmitted from rodents to humans. However, the Andes virus (ANDV), a type of New World hantavirus, can also be transmitted from human to human. It is the cause of the 2026 hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship. Hantavirus can rapidly progress to a severe respiratory distress, known as hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Since there is no specific treatment or approved vaccine for hantavirus infection, early diagnosis and critical care support are essential. In cases of HCPS, depending on the severity of the infection, it is important to administer antipyretics, vasopressors, fluid therapy, cardiopulmonary support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), mechanical ventilation, and renal replacement therapy (RRT) in a timely manner. Currently, there is no approved vaccine in the United States or Europe. However, various vaccine technologies, including inactivated, DNA, mRNA, viral vector and protein-based vaccines, are in the preclinical and clinical phases. Preventive actions, including patient isolation and physical distancing, are crucial to avoiding widespread transmission.

Keywords Hantavirus, Andes virus (ANDV), The 2026 Outbreak, Cruise ship, Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) ​Background Hantavirus (HTNV) is a spherical, enveloped, negative- sense, single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) virus that belongs to the Hantaviridae family and the Bunyavirales order. It has relatively great epidemic potential [1, 2]. The world­ wide burden of hantavirus is estimated as 10,000 to over 100,000 infections annually, and the largest burden of hantavirus is in Asia and Europe. The United States America has reported less than 1000 cases of hantavirus annually and hundreds of hantavirus cardiopulmonary cases (HCPS) cases have been reported in the Ameri­ cas [3]. It is characterized as a fatal zoonotic pathogen that is commonly transmitted from rodents to humans through contact with the feces, urine, or saliva of the Page 2 of 11 Ghasemiyeh and Mohammadi-Samani Virology Journal (2026) 23:208 infected rodents, or contact with contaminated surfaces [4, 5]. Humans are generally considered as dead-end hosts for hantavirus infections. Therefore, due to the high case fatality ratio, it cannot be readily transmitted human-to-human [2]; however, Andes virus (ANDV), Orthohantavirus andesense, is the only type of hantavi­ rus that can be transmitted human-to-human following prolonged and close contact [6, 7]. This can be attributed to its incubation period of 7–42 days (with a median of 18 days) [8, 9] and the possibility of pre-symptomatic or early symptomatic transmission. Since ANDV RNA has been detected in blood, respiratory secretions, urine, and semen, in addition to being airborne, it could be trans­ mitted through mucosal or respiratory exposure, as well [10]. ANDV was first diagnosed in Argentina in 1995 in a patient who presented with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) and ultimately died from the infection. ANDV lineages have been diagnosed and categorized based on amino acid and nucleotide differences, as well as S-segment data [11]. The ANDV is known to cause super-spreading events in Argentina. Overall, ANDV is considered a highly lethal virus, with case fatality ratios reaching 50% [10, 12]. The 2026 Andes virus outbreak Recently, on May 2, 2026, new cases of ANDV were reported to the WHO. The patients were traveling on the Dutch-flagged cruise ship MV Hondius, which car­ ried 147 crew members and passengers from 23 differ­ ent countries at that time, and 34 passengers and crew members had disembarked earlier. The patients were presented with severe respiratory distress and were hos­ pitalized. They initially presented with fever and gastro­ intestinal (GI) symptoms, which quickly progressed to pneumonia, shock, and acute respiratory distress syn­ drome (ARDS) [13]. The date of notification of the cluster of passengers with severe respiratory illness to WHO was 2 May 2026, while the date of laboratory confirmation of Andes virus infection, based on PCR positivity for Andes virus, was 4–6 May 2026 [13, 14]. As of July 2, 2026, 13 cases of ANDV infection had been detected on the cruise ship (12 confirmed and one probable cases). Unfortu­ nately, three patients have died (two confirmed and one probable case), resulting in a case fatality ratio of 23% [14]. One hypothesis is that the first case was contaminated by a rodent before boarding the cruise ship and that the others became infected through human-to-human trans­ mission following close and prolonged contact. No new lineages or viral genome diversity were detected among the infected passengers on the cruise ship, and the iso­ lated lineage was similar to that of previously detected ANDV in Argentina and Chile. However, further genomic sequencing and epidemiological evaluations are required to confirm these findings [15]. A recent study reported that the L protein (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp)) of ANDV showed about 72% amino acid iden­ tity and 70 to 75% identity of catalytic residues with the Old World hantavirus. Additionally, the polymerase core domain of the ANDV showed 75 to 80% identity with the hantavirus [16]. Since the ANDV incubation period can last up to 6 weeks, passengers were asked to quarantine for 42 days after disembarking from the cruise ship and entering their home country [15]. The 2026 ANDV outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hon­ dius confirmed the international transportation sys­ tem’s susceptibility to infectious diseases that evolve and spread through human-to-human contact following close and prolonged exposure. Factors that contribute to the emergence of infectious diseases on cruise ships include restricted spaces, overcrowding, inadequate ventilation, and limited access to medical and intensive care settings. To prevent future outbreaks, passengers from hantavi­ rus-endemic areas must be screened before boarding. In addition, controlling rodents on ships and in harbors would help prevent further outbreaks. Furthermore, implementing approved protocols for preventing infec­ tious diseases in international transportation systems is crucial. Finally, global cooperation in the early man­ agement of urgent medical conditions in international waters is essential [17]. Based on previous and current ANDV outbreaks and the low probability of ANDV transmission per case, widespread human-to-human transmission is unlikely. However, human-to-human transmission can occur, and the transmission rate increases with a higher viral load, as seen in the largest ANDV outbreak in Argentina from 2018 to 2019. Transmission may also increase with par­ ticipation in large group gatherings in confined areas. ANDV can be transmitted through direct contact with contaminated surfaces or individuals. It can also be trans­ mitted via airborne transmission by inhaling infectious respiratory particles (IRPs) or through-the-air transmis­ sion by direct deposition of IRPs in facial mucosal areas. Nevertheless, ANDV is not categorized as a highly air­ borne transmissible pathogen. Additionally, the ANDV incubation period is 15–24 days. Therefore, releasing passengers from quarantine after 42 days results in a 96% probability of safe release and reduces the rate of further human-to-human transmission after unboarding [18]. The current ANDV outbreak on the cruise ship MV Hondius is a multi-country outbreak. Following close and prolonged exposure in an overcrowded and confined area, human-to-human transmission has been occurred, resulting in a reproductive number of 0.7 [18]. The pre­ vious ANDV outbreak occurred in Argentina from 2018 to 2019. There, human-to-human transmission occurred with a median reproductive numbers of 2.12 and 0.96 Page 3 of 11 Ghasemiyeh and Mohammadi-Samani Virology Journal (2026) 23:208 before and after infection control, respectively. The causative strain of the 2018–2019 ANDV outbreak was Epuyén/18–19, which was similar to the wild type [12]. In the 2026 outbreak, it has been proposed that a passenger was contaminated by a rodent, and that the subsequent outbreak occurred through human-to-human viral trans­ mission [18]. During the 2018–2019 outbreak, human- to-human transmission occurred following exposure to three infected patients, known as super-spreaders, at a large social gathering. This resulted in the largest ANDV outbreak to date [12]. The case fatality ratio of the 2026 ANDV outbreak is 23% [18], while the case fatality ratio of the 2018–2019 outbreak in Argentina was approxi­ mately 32% [12]. Overall, although ANDV has been known to cause a neglected zoonotic disorder for many years, the 2026 outbreak revealed that it could potentially become a global public health concern in the future [19]. Currently, the risk of a public health crisis or a world­ wide hantavirus pandemic is considered very low. However, preventive actions and global awareness are required to prevent its transmission and spread through­ out nations [6]. Preventive actions include regular hand­ washing, physical distancing, patient isolation, rodent control (especially in rural areas), and decontaminating environments contaminated by the saliva, urine, or feces of infected rodents to prevent the aerosolized transmis­ sion of hantavirus [20]. Risk assessments should also be conducted before traveling to endemic regions. Due to the possible airborne transmission of ANDV, healthcare workers should wear special clothing and N95 or filtering face piece 2 (FFP2) masks [21]. Pathogenesis Hantavirus infection can lead to two main complications: hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which is more prevalent in the Americas, especially Argen­ tina and Chile, and hemorrhagic fever with renal syn­ drome (HFRS), which is prevalent in Europe and Asia [22]. HCPS, formerly called hantavirus pulmonary syn­ drome (HPS), is typically characterized by fever, myalgia, weakness, and a rapid progression to ARDS, pulmonary edema, interstitial edema, hypotension, and shock. Its pathogenesis is shown in Fig. 1. HFRS is characterized by fever, acute renal failure, thrombocytopenia, hemor­ rhagic disorders, circulatory collapse, and hypotension [22]. The major target organs in HCPS and HFRS are the lungs and kidneys, respectively. The main pathogenesis of HCPS and HFRS is enhanced microvascular perme­ ability in targeted organs, i.e. the lungs in HCPS and the kidneys in HFRS. Endothelial cells are considered as the primary targets of hantavirus. Therefore, endothelial dys­ function and capillary leak syndrome may lead to HCPS and HFRS. In addition, immune-mediated mechanisms can play a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of HCPS and Fig. 1 A schematic view of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) pathogenesis Page 4 of 11 Ghasemiyeh and Mohammadi-Samani Virology Journal (2026) 23:208 infection. IgG antibodies develop in a short while after IgM antibodies appear, i.e. 3 to 7 days after symptom initiation, and remain for years. Therefore, IgG antibod­ ies cannot be used to diagnose the early stages of ANDV infection [25]. Optimized standard operating procedures (SOPs) and adherence to infection control guidelines are essential for the collection, storage, and shipment of blood specimens and should be performed by trained personnel for biosafety considerations [25]. It should be noted that some RT-PCR-positive cases were asymptom­ atic and that viremia can occur before symptoms appear [19]. Differential diagnoses of ANDV infection, especially during the prodromal phase, include influenza, SARS- CoV-2 infection (i.e., COVID-19), viral pneumonia, atypical pneumonia, yellow fever, dengue, leptospirosis, endocarditis with pulmonary edema, sepsis with ARDS, and arenaviruses infection [25]. Clinical manifestations As previously mentioned, hantavirus can be associ­ ated with HCPS and HFRS, which can be deadly [4, 5]. Hantavirus can lead to thrombocytopenia, increased vascular permeability, and activation of the adaptive and innate immune responses [2]. The initial symptoms of HCPS usually present 1 to 8 weeks after viral exposure. These symptoms are somewhat non-specific and include chills, fever, GI upset, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, head­ ache, dizziness, and myalgia. However, they can progress suddenly to ARDS, hypotension, and shock [13]. Unfor­ tunately, hantaviruses have relatively high case fatality ratios in humans [26, 27]. It has been reported that the case fatality ratio of hantavirus infections in Asia and Europe is less than 1% up to 15%, while the case fatality ratio in the Americas is up to 50% [9]. Figure 2 shows a schematic view of the structure, transmission, and clini­ cal signs and symptoms of hantavirus. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis reported the following prognostic factors for severe hantavirus infections: female gender; age over 18 years old; living in rural areas due to contact with rodents; pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiographs; underlying diseases, particularly those with increased serum creatinine and hematocrit values; and signs of bleeding. Therefore, dur­ ing the patient screening and evaluation process, paying special attention to these risk factors is crucial to provid­ ing the required supportive and intensive care for these relatively high-risk patients [26]. In patients with severe HCPS, ECMO can be life-saving [6]. In selected cohorts treated in experienced centers in the USA, Argentina, and Chile, ECMO-supported survival in patients with HCPS has ranged from approximately 60% to 75% [28]. HFRS [23]. In this regard, T cell activation, particularly CD8+ T cell activation, has been reported during the acute phases of HFRS and HCPS. Additionally, immuno­ blasts have been observed in the circulatory systems of HCPS patients experiencing shock or pulmonary edema. Furthermore, patients with fatal HCPS have high levels of cytokine-releasing cells in their lung tissues. This results in the production of numerous cytokines, including interleukin 2 (IL-2), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin 6 (IL-6), and interferon gamma (IFN- γ). High levels of TNF-α can lead to capillary leakage, pulmonary edema, and shock, further enhancing case fatality ratios. Also, high levels of IL-2 may lead to increased vascular permeability [23]. In general, HCPS has three phases: [1] the prodromal phase, which presents with non-specific flu-like symptoms; [2] the cardiopulmonary phase, which is associated with the enhanced permeability of pulmo­ nary capillaries and hemodynamic compromise, which can lead to cardiogenic shock in severe cases; and [3] the convalescent or recovery phase [24]. 1. Diagnosis Since there is no specific antiviral agent for managing ANDV infection, early diagnosis and management are crucial. Laboratory testing is helpful for early diagnosis, disease management, and outbreak control. Reverse tran­ scription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) can detect ANDV infection by identifying viral RNA in whole blood specimens collected from patients. RT-PCR can confirm ANDV infection during the asymptomatic phase (median of 18 days) or the prodromal phase (2–8 days) [25]. Diag­ nosis can be confirmed using serological techniques (IgM and IgG assays using the chemiluminescence immu­ noassay (CLIA) technique) in conjunction with clinical presentations [25]. Supportive care, including ECMO, renal replace­ ment therapy (RRT), and vasopressor administration, depends on the stage of the disease and the presenting symptoms [16]. analysis.background: Hantavirus is a fatal zoonotic pathogen commonly transmitted from rodents, but Andes virus (ANDV) can also spread human‑to‑human, prompting a 2026 outbreak on a cruise ship.
analysis.main_directions: The review covers ANDV pathogenesis, severe respiratory syndrome (HCPS), clinical progression, supportive pharmacologic care, and emerging vaccine platforms.
analysis.current_state: No approved vaccine exists; early diagnosis and intensive supportive care (antipyretics, vasopressors, ECMO, RRT) are critical, with a 23% case‑fatality ratio reported in the cruise‑ship cluster.
analysis.gaps: Evidence gaps include lack of specific antiviral therapy, limited data on human‑to‑human transmission dynamics, and uncertainty about optimal supportive interventions.
analysis.future_research: Future work should focus on vaccine development, rapid diagnostic tools, clinical trials of advanced supportive therapies, and strengthened isolation and distancing policies to curb spread.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantavirus is a fatal zoonotic pathogen commonly transmitted from rodents, but Andes virus (ANDV) can also spread human‑to‑human, prompting a 2026 outbreak on a cruise ship. Main directions: The review covers ANDV pathogenesis, severe respiratory syndrome (HCPS), clinical progression, supportive pharmacologic care, and emerging vaccine platforms. Current state: No approved vaccine exists; early diagnosis and intensive supportive care (antipyretics, vasopressors, ECMO, RRT) are critical, with a 23% case‑fatality ratio reported in the cruise‑ship cluster. Gaps: Evidence gaps include lack of specific antiviral therapy, limited data on human‑to‑human transmission dynamics, and uncertainty about optimal supportive interventions. Future research: Future work should focus on vaccine development, rapid diagnostic tools, clinical trials of advanced supportive therapies, and strengthened isolation and distancing policies to curb spread.

papers.title: Burning down the mouse: Effects of wildfire and post-fire reseeding on Sin Nombre virus prevalence in its reservoir host
papers.abstract: Abstract Worldwide, physical habitats and biological communities are being reshaped by wildfire. Such changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. Open research statement To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript.

Silva1,2*, Frances M. Twohig3, Matthew E. Gompper2, Robert A. Nofchissey3, Aaron 5 C. Young2, Steven B. Bradfute3 and Kathryn A. Hanley1 6 7 Author affiliations: 8 1 Department of Biology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88003, USA 9 2 Department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, New Mexico State University, Las 10 Cruces, NM 88003, USA 11 3 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico Health 12 Sciences Center, Albuquerque, NM, 87106 USA 13 * Corresponding author; cnsilva@nmsu.edu 14 15 Open research statement: To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place 16 all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript. 17 Keywords: Sin Nombre virus, hantavirus, deer mouse, wildfire, post-fire management, disease 18 ecology, ENSO 19 20 Abstract 21 Worldwide, physical habitats and biological communities are being reshaped by wildfire. Such 22 changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those 23 focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. 24 Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen 25 circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence 26 and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, 27 using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New 28 Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the 29 effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection 30 probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded 31 sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed 32 canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative 33 abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either 34 burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not 35 differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any 36 strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an 37 El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that 38 were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased 39 significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support 40 increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire 41 management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study 42 should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. 43 Introduction 44 Wildfires are increasing in both severity and frequency across the globe, driven by rising 45 temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns (Cunningham et al., 2024; Dennison et al., 2014; 46 Salguero et al., 2020; Westerling et al., 2006). Wildfires can dramatically reshape natural 47 landscapes through reduction of ground litter, loss of canopy cover, and transformation of soil 48 chemistry, among many other effects (Bansal, 2025). Following a wildfire, managers may 49 implement strategies to prevent soil erosion, such as reseeding, replanting, mulching or chemical 50 treatments. These interventions may alleviate some negative effects of wildfire, such as runoff or 51 mudslides, but may exacerbate others, such as alteration of plant communities (Keeley, 2004). 52 These wholesale changes in both burned and remediated landscapes have the potential to alter 53 the transmission of pathogens among wildlife, thereby altering the risk of pathogen spillover to 54 humans. In an increasingly flammable world, it is critical to gain an understanding of the effects 55 of fire on wildlife infection. 56 Albery et al. (2021) have laid out multiple, intersecting mechanisms by which the consequences 57 of wildfire could influence the exposure of wildlife to pathogens. At the nexus of this framework 58 are the impacts of fire on host movement and resource availability. For directly-transmitted 59 pathogens, wildfire may enhance inter-individual contact rates, and therefore transmission, via 60 degradation of habitat complexity, concentration of existing resources, or production of resource 61 pulses that support increases in the host population density. Alternatively, wildfire may reduce 62 contact rates through habitat fragmentation, fire-mediated mortality, or production of resource 63 pulses that disincentivize host foraging movements (Fay et al., 2025; Tonelli et al., 2026). Thus, 64 wildfire may shape infection dynamics through multiple, potentially opposing, mechanisms. 65 Although Albery et al. (2021) did not consider post-fire mitigation, it is clear that some 66 management strategies may also affect host movement and host density. In particular, post-fire 67 reseeding provides a large pulse in resources for granivores that may drive surges in their 68 populations, and the plants that sprout from supplementary seeds may alter vegetation structure 69 and plant community composition. 70 To date, the majority of studies investigating the impact of wildfire on the frequency of wildlife 71 infection have focused on ectoparasites (reviewed in Scasta, 2015) or on proxies of disease risk, 72 such as corticosteroid levels (Hing et al., 2017), immune function, or immune proteomes (Black 73 et al., 2017; Bowen et al., 2015) rather than directly measuring wildfire impacts on pathogen 74 prevalence. Two notable exceptions are work by Ecke et al. (2019) and Furtado et al. (2023). 75 The former showed that wildfire-induced thermal stress may increase host susceptibility to 76 parasitic infection in Tropidurus oreadicus lizards, and the latter demonstrated that reduced 77 habitat complexity correlated with increased Puumala virus (PUUV, Orthohantavirus 78 puumalaense) prevalence in bank voles. 79 In the current study, we investigated the effects of wildfires and post-fire management in 80 northern New Mexico on Sin Nombre virus (SNV, Orthohantavirus sinnombreense) infection of 81 western deer mice (Peromyscus sonoriensis). Western deer mice serve as a major reservoir host 82 of SNV. Increases in SNV prevalence in deer mice are associated with increases in spillover of 83 the virus to humans, in whom it can cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) with a 84 fatality rate of ~35% (Childs et al., 1994; Center for Disease Control, 2024). SNV circulation in 85 deer mice is sensitive to ecological perturbations that alter mouse density, as the virus is 86 transmitted via direct, aggressive contacts, primarily among adult males, that can increase with 87 density (Mills et al., 1997; Pearce-Duvet et al., 2006). In particular, SNV prevalence in deer 88 mouse populations, and subsequent human outbreaks, have been linked to El Niño Southern 89 Oscillation (ENSO) events, which drive increased precipitation throughout the western United 90 States, leading to mast seed production of piñon trees, a food resource pulse that supports 91 increases in deer mouse density (Carver et al., 2015; Parmenter et al., 1993). While ENSO 92 cycles provide a well-established example of how ecological perturbations can alter the SNV 93 system within deer mice, wildfire and post-fire mitigation may act via similar mechanisms. 94 Populations of Peromyscus spp. have generally been shown to increase following both wild and 95 prescribed fires, likely due to release of competition with members of their guild and increased 96 foraging efficiency in the absence of ground litter (reviewed in Jones, 1992; Zwolak et al., 2010). 97 Such increases in host abundance could accelerate SNV transmission and enhance prevalence. 98 Consistent with this paradigm, Mull et al. (2023) reported that more rodents were seropositive 99 for orthohantaviruses in burned prairies in the U.S. compared to clear cut or unmanaged control 100 areas, and Gheler-Costa et al. (2022) found Brazilian Sigmodontinae rodents experienced much 101 faster population growth and were more frequently positive for orthohantaviruses after sugarcane 102 harvest fires than in areas where fire had been suppressed. However, fire effects are unlikely to 103 be universal. Sharp Bowman et al. (2017) found that fires in the Great Basin, USA decreased 104 Peromyscus population sizes, suggesting that severe fires may result in unsuitable habitat and 105 decreased host abundance. Post-fire aerial reseeding may further modify these relationships. By 106 providing an artificial resource pulse, reseeding may act in an analogous fashion to resource 107 pulses associated with ENSO cycles, supporting higher densities of deer mice and elevating SNV 108 prevalence (Figure 1). However, as reseeding also alters habitat composition and vegetation 109 structure, its effects may not be mediated solely by host density. 110 These previous studies of deer mouse and SNV dynamics offer the rationale for the central 111 hypothesis of this study, that changes in habitat structure and resource availability mediated by 112 wildfire and post-fire management will lead to higher SNV prevalence within deer mouse 113 populations via their effects on deer mouse abundance. Our study was conducted in northern 114 New Mexico in the southwest United States, a region that has been ravaged by wildfires during 115 the last decade. We tested several predictions stemming from our central hypothesis, namely: (1) 116 relative abundance of deer mice and prevalence of SNV in deer mice would be higher in sites 117 that had recently burned in a wildfire compared to ecologically-matched, unburned control sites 118 (Figure 1A and 1B), and (2) relative abundance of deer mice and SNV prevalence would be 119 higher in sites that had recently burned in a wildfire and been reseeded post-fire compared to 120 burned sites that had not been reseeded and unburned sites (Figure 1D). Serendipitously, because 121 2023 was an El Niño year, we were also able to test (3) whether prevalence of SNV would 122 increase at a one-year lag following an ENSO event (Figure 1C), as has been demonstrated 123 previously in the desert southwest (Engelthaler et al., 1999; Yates et al., 2002). Additionally, we 124 tested whether two other well recognized patterns in SNV prevalence also held true in our data: 125 (4) SNV prevalence would be higher in adult male than female mice, and higher in adults than 126 juveniles (Douglass et al., 2001; Mills et al., 1997), and (5) SNV prevalence would correlate with 127 degree of wounding (Douglass et al., 2001). Finally, although we had no a priori reason to 128 expect a difference, we nonetheless tested (6) whether SNV viral load in individual mice differed 129 among burn history types. To address our predictions, we live-trapped deer mice over the 130 summers in 2023 and 2024 at areas that had burned with high intensity one or two years 131 previously and were or were not reseeded, as well as at ecologically-matched, unburned control 132 sites. SNV infection of these mice was detected via RT-qPCR of collected lung tissues. 133 134 Figure 1. Predicted effects of wildfire and resource pulses due to reseeding or an ENSO event on 135 vegetation, deer mouse abundance, and SNV prevalence in deer mice. The total number of mice 136 represent the relative abundance of deer mice in a given burn history type; red mice represent 137 SNV positive mice; black mice represent SNV negative mice. A) Independent of ENSO, we 138 predict that unburned sites will remain unchanged in vegetation structure, deer mouse 139 abundance, and SNV prevalence; B) Independent of ENSO, we predict that burned sites will 140 experience substantial vegetation loss, increased mouse abundance and a concomitant increase in 141 SNV prevalence due to wildfire; C) When ENSO occurs, we predict that burned sites will 142 experience a pulse in seed production, which in turn will support even higher levels of deer 143 mouse density than scenario B, and therefore higher SNV prevalence; D) When burned sites are 144 subject to aerial reseeding, we predict that this resource pulse will act similarly to the natural 145 resource pulse triggered by ENSO in scenario C. 146 147 Methods and Materials 148 Ethical Approvals and Permits 149 All procedures on mice were approved by the New Mexico State University Institutional Animal 150 Care and Use Committee (approval number 2404001125) and permission was given by the 151 Jemez and Pecos Las Vegas Ranger districts to trap mice within their respective national forests. 152 Field procedures were conducted following the Animal Care and Use guidelines of the American 153 Society of Mammologists (Sikes and Gannon, 2011). 154 Study Areas 155 This study was conducted in northern New Mexico (NM) (Figure 2A), an area that experiences 156 mild summer temperatures with highs averaging 290C, extreme winter temperatures dipping as 157 low as -340C, and seasonal precipitation occurring during summer monsoons and winter 158 snowstorms (Figure 3). Northern NM has experienced multiple large fires in the last few years, 159 including the two foci of this study, the Cerro Pelado fire and the Hermit’s Peak/Calf Canyon 160 fire. The Cerro Pelado fire, which began in April 2022, seven miles east of the village of Jemez 161 Springs, NM, USA (350 46’ 30” latitude, -1060 35’ 4” longitude), was a mixed severity fire that 162 burned over 45,000 acres (Figure 2B). The Hermit’s Peak fire started as a prescribed burn but 163 was declared a wildfire on April 6, 2022. The Calf Canyon fire started as a pile burn holdover in 164 January and re-emerged in April 2022. The two fires eventually merged into one, becoming the 165 largest and most devastating fire in New Mexico state history. The Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon 166 complex fire burned over 341,000 acres in the Santa Fe National Forest and surrounding areas 167 near Las Vegas, NM (105°20'19" latitude, 35°48'59" longitude; Figure 2D). 168 To assess the impact of habitat alterations due to fire and post-fire mitigation on relative mouse 169 abundance and SNV prevalence and viral load, mice were live-trapped at 3 sites each in areas 170 affected by the Cerro Pelado or the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire, as well as 3 ecologically- 171 matched, unburned control sites for each fire, and 2 sites that had burned and been reseeded, for 172 a total of 14 sites (Figure 2C and 2E). Trapping was initially intended to occur at the Cerro 173 Pelado fire sites in 2023 and the Hermit’s Peak-Calf Canyon fire sites in 2024 (Figure 2F). 174 However, in 2023, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) declared the 175 arrival of an El Niño event during our sampling session (NOAA, 2023). To test the impact of El 176 Niño on SNV prevalence in deer mice, the burned sites in the Cerro Pelado fire were resampled 177 in 2024 (Figure 2F); time restrictions prevented the resampling of the unburned sites. 178 Additionally, trapping was initially intended to occur at three reseeded sites, but extreme rainfall 179 washed out the road to our final reseeded site, making it inaccessible. Instead, we re-sampled the 180 site with the lowest trap success (unburned Site ‘U3’) to attempt to standardize representation 181 across all burn history types. The data from the resampled site was not treated as an independent 182 site, but as a continuation of the previous trapping iteration. 183 184 Figure 2. A) The state of New Mexico in the United States of America with locations of Cerro 185 Pelado fire (left black box) and Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon (right black box); B) Cerro Pelado 186 fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; C) Locations of burned and unburned sites. 187 Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites denoted by tree icons; D) Hermit’s Peak 188 Calf Canyon fire perimeter; sampling area denoted by red box; E) Locations of burned, 189 unburned, and reseeded sites. Burned sites represented by fire icons, unburned sites represented 190 by tree icons, reseeded sites represented by grass icons; F) Sampling timeline; “CP” stands for 191 Cerro Pelado; “HPCC” stands for Hermit’s Peak Calf Canyon. Map was created with ArcGIS 192 Pro. Icons are from Canva free edition. 193 194 Sampling Sites 195 Burned sites were constrained to areas categorized as high severity soil burn, determined by a 196 post-fire BAER (burned action emergency response) survey conducted by the U.S. Forest 197 Service (NM Fire Info 2022). To select burned sites, first 100 random points were generated 198 within high severity burned areas that were within 500 meters of a road and spaced at least 250 199 meters apart. A buffer of 100 meters was created around the 100 points, and sites for which 200 buffered areas were not completely within a high severity burn were excluded.
