Silva1,2*, Frances M. Twohig3, Matthew E. Gompper2, Robert A. Nofchissey3, Aaron 5 C. Young2, Steven B. Bradfute3 and Kathryn A. Hanley1 6 7 Author affiliations: 8 1 Department of Biology, New Mexico State University, Las Cruces, NM 88003, USA 9 2 Department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, New Mexico State University, Las 10 Cruces, NM 88003, USA 11 3 Department of Internal Medicine, Center for Global Health, University of New Mexico Health 12 Sciences Center, Albuquerque, NM, 87106 USA 13 * Corresponding author; cnsilva@nmsu.edu 14 15 Open research statement: To ensure transparency and reproducibility, the authors pledge to place 16 all data and any novel code into Dryad upon acceptance of the manuscript. 17 Keywords: Sin Nombre virus, hantavirus, deer mouse, wildfire, post-fire management, disease 18 ecology, ENSO 19 20 Abstract 21 Worldwide, physical habitats and biological communities are being reshaped by wildfire. Such 22 changes have obvious potential to alter pathogen ecology, yet few studies, outside of those 23 focused on ectoparasites, have tested the effects of wildfire on pathogen prevalence in wildlife. 24 Even fewer have focused on the impacts of strategies for post-fire remediation on pathogen 25 circulation. Here, we investigated the effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on the prevalence 26 and viral load of Sin Nombre virus (SNV) infection in its reservoir host, the western deer mouse, 27 using a study design of matched burned, unburned, and post-burn reseeded sites in northern New 28 Mexico. In total, we screened 411 individual deer mice for SNV via RT-qPCR and analyzed the 29 effect of wildfire and wildfire mitigation on relative mouse abundance, individual infection 30 probability, site-level prevalence and viral load. Relative abundance was highest at reseeded 31 sites, and model selection indicated that habitat structure – particularly the gradient from closed 32 canopy to open-herbaceous habitat, was consistently associated with increased relative 33 abundance. Similarly, SNV prevalence was significantly higher in reseeded sites than either 34 burned or unburned sites but did not differ in burned versus unburned sites. Viral load did not 35 differ between burn history types, and zero-inflated gamma hurdle models did not identify any 36 strong predictors of viral load. Serendipitously, we were also able to investigate the impacts of an 37 El Nino Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle on patterns of infection in a subsample of sites that 38 were studied during and one year after an ENSO year and found that SNV prevalence increased 39 significantly post-ENSO. Both reseeding and ENSO deliver resource pulses that can support 40 increases in mouse density and thereby enhance SNV transmission. The impacts of post-fire 41 management practices on SNV prevalence in its reservoir host that were revealed in this study 42 should be considered when implementing such strategies and when utilizing treated areas. 43 Introduction 44 Wildfires are increasing in both severity and frequency across the globe, driven by rising 45 temperatures and shifting rainfall patterns (Cunningham et al., 2024; Dennison et al., 2014; 46 Salguero et al., 2020; Westerling et al., 2006). Wildfires can dramatically reshape natural 47 landscapes through reduction of ground litter, loss of canopy cover, and transformation of soil 48 chemistry, among many other effects (Bansal, 2025). Following a wildfire, managers may 49 implement strategies to prevent soil erosion, such as reseeding, replanting, mulching or chemical 50 treatments. These interventions may alleviate some negative effects of wildfire, such as runoff or 51 mudslides, but may exacerbate others, such as alteration of plant communities (Keeley, 2004). 52 These wholesale changes in both burned and remediated landscapes have the potential to alter 53 the transmission of pathogens among wildlife, thereby altering the risk of pathogen spillover to 54 humans. In an increasingly flammable world, it is critical to gain an understanding of the effects 55 of fire on wildlife infection. 56 Albery et al. (2021) have laid out multiple, intersecting mechanisms by which the consequences 57 of wildfire could influence the exposure of wildlife to pathogens. At the nexus of this framework 58 are the impacts of fire on host movement and resource availability. For directly-transmitted 59 pathogens, wildfire may enhance inter-individual contact rates, and therefore transmission, via 60 degradation of habitat complexity, concentration of existing resources, or production of resource 61 pulses that support increases in the host population density. Alternatively, wildfire may reduce 62 contact rates through habitat fragmentation, fire-mediated mortality, or production of resource 63 pulses that disincentivize host foraging movements (Fay et al., 2025; Tonelli et al., 2026). Thus, 64 wildfire may shape infection dynamics through multiple, potentially opposing, mechanisms. 65 Although Albery et al. (2021) did not consider post-fire mitigation, it is clear that some 66 management strategies may also affect host movement and host density. In particular, post-fire 67 reseeding provides a large pulse in resources for granivores that may drive surges in their 68 populations, and the plants that sprout from supplementary seeds may alter vegetation structure 69 and plant community composition. 70 To date, the majority of studies investigating the impact of wildfire on the frequency of wildlife 71 infection have focused on ectoparasites (reviewed in Scasta, 2015) or on proxies of disease risk, 72 such as corticosteroid levels (Hing et al., 2017), immune function, or immune proteomes (Black 73 et al., 2017; Bowen et al., 2015) rather than directly measuring wildfire impacts on pathogen 74 prevalence. Two notable exceptions are work by Ecke et al. (2019) and Furtado et al. Western deer mice serve as a major reservoir host 82 of SNV. In particular, SNV prevalence in deer 88 mouse populations, and subsequent human outbreaks, have been linked to El Niño Southern 89 Oscillation (ENSO) events, which drive increased precipitation throughout the western United 90 States, leading to mast seed production of piñon trees, a food resource pulse that supports 91 increases in deer mouse density (Carver et al., 2015; Parmenter et al., 1993). papers.title: DNA and mRNA Vaccines Against Hantaviruses: Antigen Design, Delivery Strategies and Translational Progress
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are members of the Hantaviridae family, which can cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). At present, no specific antiviral treatment is available for hantavirus infection, while licensed hantavirus vaccines are restricted to a limited number of countries in Asia. This review summarizes recent advances in hantavirus DNA and messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, focusing on antigen design, delivery systems, immunogenicity, safety and translational development. Peer-reviewed studies published primarily within the past 10 years were evaluated together with available hantavirus vaccine trials registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, with emphasis on Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Andes virus (ANDV). DNA vaccine candidates have demonstrated immunogenicity in preclinical and early clinical studies, with an acceptable safety profile. mRNA vaccines represent a newer approach with promising preclinical evidence of humoral and cellular immune responses. However, they have not yet been evaluated clinically. Studies have also reported the potential for varying degrees of cross-protection between hantavirus species, although protection remains limited by antigenic diversity. Overall, current evidence supports further development of nucleic acid-based hantavirus vaccines, particularly multivalent strategies, with emphasis on standardized evaluation and clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Andes Virus: From Transmission Dynamics to Pandemic Potential.
papers.abstract: Background Andes virus (ANDV) has recently emerged as a significant public health concern following a multi-country outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship in April 2026, with 13 identified cases and three deaths among passengers and crew. Methods We reviewed available literature from PubMed and Google Scholar databases and searched international health agencies, including the World Health Organisation and national public health authorities, for current outbreak information and up-to-date epidemiological data. Results ANDV is a zoonotic orthohantavirus endemic in southern Chile and Argentina, with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir. Approximately 300 cases of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome occur annually in the Americas. The virus causes severe disease through endothelial dysfunction and vascular leakage, resulting in rapidly progressive pulmonary edema and shock. Human-to-human transmission is characteristic of ANDV and occurs through respiratory and salivary routes during prolonged close contact. Clinical presentation includes nonspecific prodromal symptoms followed by rapid cardiopulmonary deterioration. Diagnosis relies on serological assays and RT-qPCR. Management is predominantly supportive, emphasising hemodynamic monitoring and early consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe cases. Conclusions Despite ANDV's severity and high mortality, its epidemic potential seems to be low. However, the recent outbreak underscores the importance of international surveillance coordination and rapid diagnostic capabilities for emerging zoonotic infections.

papers.title: Hantavirus outbreak on a cruise ship: Public health challenges.
papers.abstract: •A rare hantavirus outbreak on MV Hondius in May 2026 caused 8 cases and 3 deaths.•Cruise ship confined spaces and HVAC systems facilitated aerosol transmission.•Jurisdictional disputes delayed critical medical evacuations.•Lack of isolation and diagnostics exposed cruise ship medical vulnerabilities.•Pathogen research and robust maritime emergency protocols are needed.
